scenes.what_happens: During their Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield pass the neglected door, and Enfield announces that it is connected with an odd story.
Enfield recounts how Hyde tramples a child, pays her family with a cheque signed by a respectable man, and spends the night before the cheque is verified.
Enfield explains why he calls the building Black Mail House and describes its secretive appearance while he and Utterson continue walking.
Utterson presses Enfield for Hyde’s name and description, reveals that he knows the respectable cheque drawer, and agrees to keep the matter secret.
Utterson intercepts Hyde, demands to see his face, and is left horrified by the man’s appearance and behavior.
On their Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at the door and decide to enter the court to look toward Jekyll’s windows.
Jekyll’s sudden look of terror drives the two men away in silence, and they acknowledge their shared horror in the neighbouring thoroughfare.

state_changes.change: The child is trampled and left screaming, though the doctor says she is not much the worse.
Hyde provides ten pounds in gold and a cheque for the balance as payment to the child’s family.
The child’s family, the doctor, Enfield, and Hyde spend the rest of the night in Enfield’s chambers.
The bank verifies that the cheque is genuine.
Utterson reveals that he already knows the name of the other party, the respectable cheque drawer.
Enfield confirms that Hyde still possesses the key and that Enfield saw him use it less than a week earlier.
Utterson and Enfield agree never to refer to the matter again.
Utterson identifies Hyde by description and sees his face, gaining direct knowledge of him.
Utterson tells Enfield that he once saw Hyde and shared Enfield’s repulsion.
Enfield reveals that he discovered the door was a back way to Dr. Jekyll’s.
Utterson becomes uneasy about Jekyll and decides to enter the court to look toward the windows.
Jekyll’s expression changes from a smile to abject terror and despair, and the window is thrust down.
Utterson and Enfield become pale and display shared horror after leaving the court.

It is where Enfield’s story of Hyde’s violence and the suspicious cheque begins, where Utterson first confronts Hyde, and where Utterson and Enfield later witness Jekyll’s terror. The site anchors the mystery of the relationship between Hyde and Jekyll.

views.prompt: THE FOCUS OF THE PICTURE IS a sinister two-storey block of building thrusting its gable forward onto a narrow London by-street, its facade filling the whole frame from the left edge to the right edge. The upper storey is one flat, blank, unbroken forehead of discoloured, damp-stained grey plaster, a single smooth plaster surface running from the eaves down to the door lintel and across the full width of the frame. The lower storey holds one low door alone, blistered and distained, its brown paint peeling in scabs, set in a shallow sunken recess above two worn stone steps, the plaster around it scratched and grimy. Wet black cobbles in the foreground, a cold iron gas lamp at the kerb on the right, grey fog on a dim London morning, a sense of prolonged and sordid negligence.
